content.overview: Strict liability under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher arises when a person, for a non-natural use of land, brings and keeps a dangerous thing likely to do mischief if it escapes, and it escapes and causes damage. Liability is strict but not absolute: established exceptions apply.

sections.heading: Elements
sections.body: 1. Dangerous thing brought onto land. 2. Non-natural use of land. 3. Escape. 4. Damage. Fault need not be proved once the rule is attracted, subject to exceptions.

sections.heading: Exceptions
sections.body: Classic exceptions: plaintiff's default; consent (volenti); act of a stranger; act of God; statutory authority. These exceptions mark the difference from Indian absolute liability.

sections.heading: Indian reception
sections.body: Indian courts have applied Rylands with care about what counts as non-natural use. For hazardous industry harm to the community, prefer the absolute liability analysis in M.C. Mehta rather than stretching Rylands.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead the Rylands elements and identify or exclude exceptions. Evidence focuses on use, escape, and damage, not only on reasonable care. Distinguish claims better framed as negligence or statutory environmental liability.
